Oded the Wanderer as an early silent film about childhood, travel, and national feeling.

sources.title: Oded the Wanderer, 1933 | Primary Sources | Education at the National Library of Israel
Cultural Life in Eretz Israel (Cinema, Opera, Ballet) | Recording | Nathan Axelrod 1905-1987 interviewee

storyBeats: In 1932, Haim Halachmi founded the Workers of Eretz Israel Studios, creating a local production base for Hebrew-language filmmaking.
Halachmi and Nathan Axelrod produced Oded HaNoded on a very low budget as a silent feature film.
The film told a simple story about a boy who gets lost while walking with classmates and discovers scenic places around the country.
A January 26, 1933 poster announced the film as the first Hebrew feature film and emphasized that its script, photography, landscape, and actors were all Hebrew.
The Zion Cinema in Jerusalem scheduled the film for screening, showing that the production was moving from studio work to public exhibition.
The film was well received by the Yishuv, where its patriotic tone resonated with contemporary audiences.
Nathan Axelrod later said the film’s success helped trigger new film activity, with seven film companies starting work afterward.
Axelrod also recalled that the film screened across the country and earned income of 1,200 Israeli pounds.

stories.brief: Legal deposit in Israel as a publishing and preservation system with long institutional consequences.
storyBeats: Under the British Mandate, legal-deposit materials were routed to British institutions rather than to an Israeli national library system.
After the State of Israel was established, a new deposit arrangement assigned copies of publications to the State Archive, the Knesset Library, and the National Library.
In 1953, the Knesset enacted the Books Law, making deposit at the Jewish National and University Library a legal obligation for every publication in Israel.
The Library later described its legal-deposit work as part of a broader mandate to collect and preserve books, newspapers, and other publications produced in Israel.
The 2000 Books Law required publishers in Israel to deposit two copies with the National Library within a month of publication, extending the system to print and non-print formats.
The law also covered electronic publications, audio, and video media, so the deposit system was no longer limited to bound books.
In 2007, the Knesset passed the National Library Law, redefining the institution as an independent body and formalizing its public responsibilities.
The Library tied legal deposit to long-term cultural preservation and to the creation of a national record of Israeli publishing.

stories.brief: Dov Noy as a founder of Israeli folklore scholarship and archive-based cultural research.

sources.title: By Three Things a Person Is Known

storyBeats: Dov Noy was born in 1920 in Kolomyia, then in Poland, before immigrating to Eretz Israel in 1938.
During the Second World War he served in the British Army, then went to Cyprus, where he worked as a teacher and helped run cultural activity in the detention camps.
After the war he moved into formal scholarship, studied folklore in the United States, and completed a PhD in 1954 under Stith Thompson at Indiana University.
Noy then taught Jewish folk literature at the Hebrew University and later at the University of Haifa.
In 1956 he founded the Museum of Ethnology and Folklore in Haifa.
He also established the Israel Folktale Archive, described by the National Library as the largest collection of Jewish folktales in the world.
The archive record says Noy’s professional papers contain research files, drafts, lecture materials, correspondence, and documentation of his cultural work.
His archive was deposited permanently at the National Library in July 2017 by his sons.
Noy’s archive entry also notes that his archive work and scholarship contributed to his receiving the Israel Prize in literature in 2004.

stories.brief: Carmel Agrexco as a state-linked export brand in Israeli agricultural trade history.

sources.title: A comparative study of perishable agricultural produce export organizations in Israel and Turkey

storyBeats: Israel established Agrexco in 1956 as a state-linked agricultural export company to organize fresh-produce exports.
The company began operating in 1957 after the first surplus fresh agricultural exports had been organized through Tnuva Export and the Ministry of Agriculture.
Agrexco marketed produce under the internationally recognized Carmel brand, which became the company’s export identity.
Its ownership structure reflected the state-corporatist export system: the State of Israel held 50 percent, the production and marketing boards held 25 percent, and Tnuva held 25 percent.
Agrexco expanded into a central export channel for vegetables, flowers, fruits, and plants, building an organized packing and transportation system around perishable produce.
By the late 2000s, the company was handling large export volumes and had become heavily exposed to the economics of European fresh-produce markets.
In August 2008 the Israeli government approved a privatization program that required at least 51 percent of Agrexco to be offered to private investors.
The company continued operating through a global sales network and remained tied to both Israeli growers and overseas distribution centers while privatization was being pursued.
Agrexco went into liquidation in August 2011 amid heavy debts, ending its run as a state-linked export champion.
After liquidation, the Israeli court approved a purchase offer for the company, but the earlier institutional structure that had sustained the Carmel export brand was effectively over.

stories.brief: A sister stops by her brother's apartment with a dessert she wants to test for a family meal. They taste it together, compare it with the plain version they usually make, and notice the new one is less sweet than expected. One of them suggests adding a little more honey and citrus zest, while the other worries it may become too rich. After a short discussion, they adjust the topping, write down the changed amounts, and decide to bring the improved version to Sunday lunch. In the end, they have a dessert they both like, a clearer recipe, and one less thing to plan later.

stories.brief: Two neighbors in the same building decide to set up a small shared table near the entrance for books, toys, and spare houseplants. They talk with a third resident, agree on what should stay on the table, and decide to keep only clean and useful items there. One neighbor wants it to look neat, while the other cares more about making it easy for people to take what they need. They add a simple sign, move a few extra pots to the side, and set a time to check the table again next week. In the end, the entrance feels friendlier, the items are organized, and several neighbors already start using the table.
